title: Money and pupils, fiscal 2015 to 2024
question: As enrolment fell, what happened to the money the school district takes in and spends for each pupil?
finding: Day-to-day spending by the school district and its county office rose from $777 million in fiscal 2015 to $1.24 billion in fiscal 2024 (+60%) while pupils in all San Francisco public schools went from 59,105 to 56,508 (-4%). Per pupil that is $13,154 to $21,985 (+67%); the same measure for all California school systems rose 80%. Counting only the district's own pupils, fiscal 2024 spending was $25,249 each, and all revenue was $1.53 billion. The city's children aged 5 to 17 numbered 74,976 in 2014 and 76,044 in 2023; public-school pupils were 79% and then 74% of that number.
how: Money is from the federal school-finance survey for the San Francisco Unified School District and the San Francisco County Office of Education, added together, with the district's payments to the county office taken out of revenue and total spending so they are not counted twice. Day-to-day ("current") spending leaves out construction, debt interest and payments to other school systems. Pupils are the October count of every public-school unit located in San Francisco, charter schools included, because from 2018-19 the federal files list charter schools as districts of their own: the district's own count falls by 7,765 in that one year while the all-San-Francisco count moves by -107. The California lines use the same construction: all school-system rows in the survey over all pupils in the State's public-school units. Children aged 5 to 17 are the Census Bureau's 1 July estimates for the county.
limits: The spending of independently run charter schools is not in the survey in any year, but their pupils are in the all-San-Francisco count, so the per-pupil level on that count is understated by roughly the charter share of pupils; the trend is not affected. Dollars are not adjusted for inflation. Public-school pupils include some four-year-olds and adults, so their share of children aged 5 to 17 is a rough guide to how many families use private schools or have left, not a count. The survey is a statistical collection, not an audit, and fiscal 2022 comes from books on which the district's auditor gave no opinion. A district where living costs are high must pay more to hire and keep staff, and one with many small schools, or with many pupils who are learning English, have disabilities or are poor, will spend more per pupil for honest reasons; none of those is measured here. Federal money to California school systems went from $8.00 billion in fiscal 2020 to $16.30 billion in fiscal 2022, the pandemic-aid years, and San Francisco's from $63.2 million to $188 million.
